# Disagreement Log — Didache Chapter 8

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Didache 8 — Fasting Days and the Lord's Prayer
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 6

---

## Disagreement 1 — v.1: "second and fifth days" — rendering the day names

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "second and fifth days of the week" |
| LOGOS | "second and fifth days of the week" |
| PNEUMA | "Mondays and Thursdays" / "Wednesdays and Fridays" |

**Issue:** The Greek uses ordinal day numbers (δευτέρα, πέμπτη), not day names. PNEUMA's rendering in modern day names is helpful for readers but loses the Greek reckoning system. The "Day of Preparation" (παρασκευή) is the technical term for Friday.
**Ruling:** Formal day numbering retained for the opposing fast days, but "Day of Preparation" retained as well (not simply "Friday"). PNEUMA's clarifications are noted in translator notes.

---

## Disagreement 2 — v.2: πειρασμός — "temptation" vs. "time of testing"

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "do not lead us into temptation" |
| LOGOS | "lead us not into temptation" |
| PNEUMA | "do not bring us to the time of testing" |

**Issue:** This is one of the most debated translation decisions in the Lord's Prayer. πειρασμός = trial, test, temptation. The word can be personal (moral temptation) or eschatological (the great tribulation). Pope Francis's 2017 revision of the Italian liturgy moved to "do not let us fall into temptation." PNEUMA's "time of testing" is interpretively rich. The traditional rendering has millennia of liturgical use.
**Ruling:** Traditional "lead us not into temptation" retained. Commentary notes the eschatological dimension of πειρασμός.

---

## Disagreement 3 — v.2: ὀφείλημα — "debt" vs. "trespass" vs. "sin"

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "debt / debtors" |
| LOGOS | "debt / debtors" |
| PNEUMA | "debts / those in debt to us" |

**Issue:** The Greek ὀφείλημα is unambiguously "debt." The traditional English liturgical form "trespasses" (from Tyndale via BCP) is a mistranslation (following Luke's "sins" rather than Matthew/Didache's "debts"). "Debts" is correct.
**Ruling:** "Debt / debtors" unanimous. All agents agree.

---

## Disagreement 4 — v.2: Doxology — inclusion and form

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "for thine is the power and the glory forever" |
| LOGOS | "for thine is the power and the glory forever" |
| PNEUMA | "for yours is the power and the glory, forever" |

**Issue:** PNEUMA uses "yours" (modern); EMET/LOGOS use "thine" (traditional). The doxology is not in Matthew's best manuscripts but IS in the Didache.
**Ruling:** "Thine is the power and the glory forever" retained (traditional form). The Didache is presenting a living liturgical text that should sound like prayer.

---

## Disagreement 5 — v.2: "hallowed" vs. "may your name be held holy"

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "hallowed be thy name" |
| LOGOS | "hallowed be thy name" |
| PNEUMA | "may your name be held holy" |

**Issue:** "Hallowed" (ἁγιασθήτω) is an aorist passive — "let it be made holy/sanctified." PNEUMA's "may your name be held holy" is more transparent but loses the traditional form.
**Ruling:** "Hallowed be thy name" retained. Liturgical precision and tradition outweigh accessibility here; this prayer is the community's living liturgy.

---

## Disagreement 6 — v.3: frequency — "three times a day" vs. "three times each day"

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "three times a day" |
| LOGOS | "three times each day" |
| PNEUMA | "three times every day" |

**Issue:** Minor stylistic difference. The Greek τρὶς τῆς ἡμέρας = three times of the day.
**Ruling:** "Three times each day" (LOGOS) adopted. Clear and natural.
